current_answer: AI job evidence just split along a line that headlines blur. Several U.S. exposure studies find weaker early-career outcomes, but a separate firm-data study using recorded AI spending reports that high-intensity U.S. adopters added total and entry-level headcount over two years. That is not a clean reversal: the firms were already growth-oriented and the study does not prove AI caused the gains. Broad U.S. postings still show little distinct AI-driven decline. Watch entry routes and actual adoption separately; neither an exposure score nor an AI purchase can forecast your job.

catalogue_card.question: Does actual AI adoption mean firms are cutting jobs?
catalogue_card.text: A new firm-spending study says heavy adopters added staff. Its selection limits keep the entry-level verdict open.

summary: A Ramp Economics Lab and Revelio Labs working-paper presentation links U.S. firm AI-vendor spending with workforce data and reports 10.2% total-headcount growth and 12% entry-level-headcount growth over two years for high-intensity adopters.

The result is associational. Ramp says the high-intensity firms were already larger, more engineering-intensive, more venture-backed and faster growing, and its proprietary sample is not the whole U.S. labor market.

A revised Stanford analysis of ADP payroll data finds U.S. workers aged 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations were about 19% below the employment level they would have reached by keeping pace with less-exposed peers through June 2026; the authors call this descriptive, not causal.

Two U.S. Census studies separately find lower early-career hires, initial employment or earnings in more AI-exposed industry-state cells or college majors. They use exposure rather than observed employer adoption.

A University of Warwick working paper finds remote-work exposure remains predictive of lower junior hiring and limited-experience ads after joint estimation, while its generative-AI coefficient often attenuates to no statistical distinction from zero.
A Federal Reserve analysis still finds little indication of a distinct AI-driven fall in broad U.S. job postings. That measure does not settle actual hires or entry outcomes.
uncertainty: No current study can tell a reader whether their own job will be lost to AI.

The central early-career findings are exposure-based, not observed-adoption experiments. Remote work, education, pre-trends, other simultaneous shocks and sample selection remain live attribution problems.

The Ramp result uses an actual spending proxy but its high-intensity adopters were different before adoption and the underlying data are proprietary; it is not a causal or economy-wide employment estimate.
Employment, hires, postings, entry-level headcount, initial earnings, hours and task use are different outcomes that can move differently.
freshness_note: Updated 15 September 2026 after adding a firm-level AI-spending and workforce counterpoint. We will revise when independent adoption studies, later cohorts or observed wage and hiring results change the balance.
